Satan's binding follows the return of Christ in Revelation 19 and is a complete removal of his deceiving activity from the earth for the millennium. The language of an abyss shut and sealed describes far more than the partial restraint seen in the present age, in which the New Testament still calls Satan a prowling lion and the god of this age. Christ's first-coming victory is real, but its full enforcement awaits his return.

At the end of the seven-year tribulation, after Christ defeats the beast at his glorious appearing, Satan is cast into the abyss for a literal thousand years. During the millennial kingdom he exerts no influence, which explains the righteousness and peace of that era. He is released briefly at its end and finally cast into the lake of fire.

Because the judgments of Revelation 6-19 fell on first-century Jerusalem and the persecuting powers, the binding in Revelation 20 describes the present age that began with Christ's victory. Satan was bound in the first century so that he can no longer prevent the nations from coming to Christ. Gentry stresses that the binding concerns deceiving the nations, not the abolition of all satanic activity.
Both postmillennial and amillennial preterists hold this view.

Satan was bound at the cross and through Christ's ministry, briefly loosed in the Jewish persecution of the church and the final crisis of the 60s, and crushed in AD 70, as Paul promised would happen soon. Full preterists say the binding, loosing and destruction all fall within the first century. Satan therefore no longer has authority over God's people.
Full preterists differ on how to map the loosing of Revelation 20:7-9 onto first-century events.

Historicists locate the binding at a datable turning point in church history. Some older interpreters saw it in the overthrow of pagan Rome under Constantine. Many later historicists placed it after the fall of the papal Antichrist, opening a future era of gospel triumph or Christ's reign.
There is no single historicist dating. Premillennial historicists (Elliott) treat the binding as future and total, like futurists.

Read in order, Revelation 19-20 places the binding after the visible return of Christ and the defeat of the beast and false prophet. Satan is therefore still active as the deceiver of the nations today. He will be fully imprisoned only in the future kingdom.

Revelation 20 opens a new cycle that returns to the beginning of the gospel age. The binding shows from heaven's side what Revelation 12 shows as the dragon's fall: by his death and exaltation Christ restrained Satan, so the gospel goes out to the nations. Satan rages against the church but cannot stop the ingathering of the elect.

Beale argues that Revelation 20:1-3 recapitulates Revelation 12, and that the binding happened at Christ's death and resurrection. Satan is restrained from deceiving the nations in the specific sense of preventing the gospel's spread and gathering them for the final war before the appointed time. Eclectic commentators who read Revelation 20 as following Revelation 19 in sequence place the binding in the future.
Beale holds the first-advent binding; Osborne holds a future binding.

The first resurrection is spiritual: believers share in Christ's resurrection through the new birth and reign with him now. The second resurrection, of the body, is the one general resurrection of just and unjust at Christ's return. This parallels Jesus' teaching about the spiritually dead hearing his voice now and all the dead rising later.
Warfield read the first resurrection as the blessedness of saints who have died and entered heaven (souls-in-heaven).

John sees souls, not bodies. Many amillennialists, following Hoekema and Riddlebarger, hold that the first resurrection is the believer's transition at death into the presence of Christ, where the faithful dead reign with him during the present age. The second, bodily resurrection comes for all at Christ's return.
Augustine and some modern amillennialists take it as regeneration (spiritual-regeneration).

The verb 'came to life' (ezesan) is used in Revelation 2:8 of Christ's bodily resurrection, and in Revelation 20 the same word must mean the same thing for both groups. Ladd and others argue it cannot be spiritual for one group and physical for the other. The first resurrection is the bodily raising of believers at Christ's return, and 'the rest of the dead' are raised after the millennium.

The first resurrection is the bodily resurrection of the righteous, which happens in stages. The church is raised at the rapture, and Old Testament and tribulation saints at Christ's glorious appearing. All of these precede the millennium; the unrighteous dead are raised a thousand years later for the great white throne judgment.

Because the millennium is the present age, the first resurrection must be a present reality. Preterist postmillennialists usually take it as spiritual resurrection with Christ through regeneration. Some preterists stress the vindication of the first-century martyrs, who had been slain by the beast and now reign with Christ.
Amillennial preterists usually hold the souls-in-heaven reading; all partial preterists expect a future bodily general resurrection.

Full preterists read resurrection language covenantally. In Max King's influential form, the dead are God's people under the old covenant, and their raising is their transformation into the new-covenant body of Christ, completed when the old order fell in AD 70. The raising of the dead out of Hades is also placed at AD 70.

Full preterists disagree whether the resurrection was corporate (King, 'collective body view') or individual and immaterial. Critics such as the contributors to When Shall These Things Be? argue that denying a future bodily resurrection departs from the creeds and from 1 Corinthians 15.

Many historicists read the first resurrection figuratively, as the revival of the cause, spirit and principles of the martyrs in a later age of gospel triumph. Edwards and Albert Barnes compare it with Ezekiel's valley of dry bones and the two witnesses rising again. Premillennial historicists instead take it as a literal bodily resurrection.
E. B. Elliott and other premillennial historicists held a bodily first resurrection (bodily-before-millennium).

Futurists take the passage at face value and in sequence. After Christ returns and destroys the beast, the faithful, including those martyred in the tribulation, are bodily raised to reign with him. The rest of the dead are raised after the thousand years.

The vision of thrones in Revelation 20:4 is set in heaven, where John sees the souls of those who died faithful. Their first resurrection is their entrance into life and rule with Christ at death. It is the heavenly counterpart to the church's suffering on earth throughout the age.

Beale argues that the first resurrection is the deceased believer's spiritual resurrection into heaven at death, which anticipates the final bodily resurrection. On this view the contrast between first and second resurrection mirrors the contrast between the first (physical) and second (spiritual) death. Eclectic commentators who are premillennial take it as bodily.
Beale holds souls-in-heaven; Osborne holds bodily-before-millennium.

Christ will return visibly and bodily at the end of the millennial era of gospel triumph. His coming brings one general resurrection, one final judgment and the new creation at the same time. Preterist postmillennialists distinguish this future coming from Christ's 'coming' in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70.

The Second Coming is a single, visible, bodily event at the end of the present age. It brings the general resurrection of believers and unbelievers, the final judgment, and the new heavens and earth together. There is no intervening earthly millennium; Scripture sets the present age directly against the age to come.

Christ will return visibly and bodily after the tribulation, in one coming, to raise his people, destroy Antichrist and reign on earth for the millennium. The final resurrection and judgment of the rest of the dead follow at its end. The church waits for one 'blessed hope', not a two-stage coming.

The Second Coming unfolds in two phases. First Christ comes for his church in the rapture, meeting believers in the air before the tribulation; then, seven years later, he comes with his saints in glory to the earth to judge the nations and set up the millennial kingdom. Dispensationalists say the two phases differ in purpose, recipients and the signs that precede them.
Pre-wrath and mid-trib dispensational premillennialists also hold a two-stage return but time the first stage differently.

Partial preterists distinguish Christ's 'coming' in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, described in texts with time indicators such as Matthew 16:28 and Matthew 26:64, from his future bodily return. On this view the Olivet Discourse and Revelation's near-time texts describe AD 70. Passages such as Acts 1:11 and 1 Corinthians 15 describe a still-future return with a bodily resurrection.
Holding that the Second Coming is still future is what separates partial preterism from full preterism.

Every New Testament promise of Christ's coming is time-bound to the first generation: some standing there would not taste death before it, and it was 'near' and 'soon'. Full preterists therefore conclude that the parousia, with the resurrection and judgment, happened in AD 70. They see it as a coming in glory and judgment that ended the old covenant age; there is no future return.

Outside historic creedal orthodoxy: the creeds confess a future return to judge the living and the dead. Critics cite Acts 1:11 and 1 Corinthians 15. Proponents reply that the creeds are subordinate to Scripture's time statements.

Historicists place Christ's return at the end of the prophetic sequence they trace through church history, after the fall of the papal Antichrist and, for postmillennial historicists, after the golden age. They expect it to be visible, bodily and still future. Christ's coming ends history in resurrection and judgment.
Premillennial historicists such as Elliott place the return before the millennium (future-premillennial).

Revelation 19 describes the future, visible return of Christ at the end of the tribulation, which leads directly into his millennial reign in Revelation 20. Futurists stress that much of Revelation still awaits fulfilment. They expect the end-time events in their literal sequence.
Most popular futurists are dispensational and add a pre-tribulational first stage (future-two-stage).

Idealists read most of Revelation symbolically, but each cycle of visions ends at the final coming of Christ in judgment and victory. They hold that Christ's personal return is a real future event, even though the book's imagery shows the timeless conflict of the age. The return is single and brings final judgment and new creation.

Eclectic interpreters see Revelation's seven parallel cycles as each ending at the final judgment. Beale reads Revelation 19:11-21 as the one future return that brings the last battle and the end of history. Premillennial eclectics place that return before a future millennium.
Osborne holds future-premillennial.

The 'catching up' of 1 Thessalonians 4 happens at the one future return of Christ. Living believers are gathered to meet him and accompany him as he comes to judge and renew the world. Postmillennialists reject a separate secret rapture.

There is no separate rapture. The 'meeting' in the air (apantesis) was a word for citizens going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him back to the city. In the same way, believers rise to meet Christ and come with him to the earth at his single return.

The church will pass through the future great tribulation and be gathered when Christ returns in glory at its end. Ladd argued that 'parousia', 'apokalypsis' and 'epiphaneia' all describe one post-tribulational coming. The church's hope is Christ's appearing, not escape from tribulation.

Christ will rapture the church before the seven-year tribulation, because the church is not appointed to wrath and is promised to be kept from the hour of trial. The rapture can happen at any moment, with no sign before it. The tribulation concerns God's dealings with Israel in Daniel's seventieth week.
Pre-tribulationism is the majority dispensational view; Marvin Rosenthal's pre-wrath view and mid-tribulationism are minority positions within premillennial futurism.

Partial preterists read the tribulation texts as fulfilled in AD 66-70, so there is no future tribulation from which the church needs to be removed. The gathering of believers in 1 Thessalonians 4 happens at Christ's future bodily return. Some read the gathering of the elect in Matthew 24:31 as the worldwide gospel mission after AD 70, not the rapture.

Paul wrote 'we who are alive' to first-century believers expecting the event in their lifetime. Full preterists therefore place the gathering to Christ at AD 70. Some read it covenantally as the church's union with Christ in the consummated kingdom; a minority (associated with Ed Stevens) hold that faithful believers were literally removed from the earth then.
Disputed even among full preterists: Don Preston argues for a covenantal fulfilment, while the literal-rapture view held by Ed Stevens is a minority.

Historicists, from the Reformers through the nineteenth century, generally treated the catching up of believers as part of Christ's one visible return at the end of the prophetic sequence. The idea of a separate pre-tribulational rapture belongs to the futurist system, not to historicism. Historicists also see the tribulation as already running through church history, so the church cannot escape it.

Most futurists place the rapture before the seven-year tribulation, so the church is absent from Revelation 4-19, where the word 'church' no longer appears. But futurism as a reading of Revelation does not settle the timing. Futurist interpreters include pre-tribulational, mid-tribulational, pre-wrath and post-tribulational views.
Ladd, Osborne and Mounce are futurist and post-tribulational; Rosenthal is pre-wrath.

Idealism is an approach to Revelation, and Revelation does not describe a separate rapture. Idealists typically read 1 Thessalonians 4 as the gathering of believers at Christ's single return. The church is pictured throughout Revelation as present on earth, suffering and overcoming.
Idealism does not itself settle the rapture question; the stance given is that of its typical (amillennial) proponents.

Beale and other eclectic interpreters find no separate rapture in Revelation. They see the church on earth in tribulation through the visions, and the saints are gathered at the final coming. Premillennial eclectics such as Osborne are post-tribulational.
Osborne holds the post-tribulational view (posttrib), which also places the gathering at Christ's return.

Many modern postmillennialists hold that the great tribulation was the catastrophe of the Jewish War, AD 66-70. Jesus tied it to the temple's desolation, flight from Judea and his own generation. It is past, not a barrier to future gospel progress, though postmillennialists still expect a brief rebellion just before the end.
Historicist postmillennialists (Edwards and the Puritans) instead spread tribulation through church history (church-history).

Amillennialists usually see Matthew 24 as speaking both of AD 70 and of the end, with the fall of Jerusalem as a type and preview of the end. Tribulation marks the whole church age. Hoekema and Riddlebarger hold that it will intensify into a final tribulation and apostasy just before Christ returns.
Some amillennialists (e.g. Jay Adams) hold the preterist AD 70 reading of Matthew 24:21.

A future great tribulation will come at the end of the age, centred on Antichrist's persecution of God's people, and the church will pass through it. Many historic premillennialists grant that the Olivet Discourse also addresses AD 70. They still hold that its climax looks beyond that to the end time.

The great tribulation is the future seven-year seventieth week of Daniel 9:27, after the church is raptured. Its second half, the great tribulation proper, begins when Antichrist breaks his covenant with Israel and sets up the abomination of desolation. It is a time of unprecedented divine judgment, focused on Israel and the nations.

The great tribulation was the Jewish War of AD 66-70, when Roman armies surrounded Jerusalem and the temple was destroyed, as Josephus describes. Jesus located it in Judea, said it would come within 'this generation', and told his hearers to flee. Revelation's tribulation is also read as the judgment on Jerusalem and the Neronic persecution.

The great tribulation of Matthew 24 and Revelation was entirely fulfilled in the events that ended in AD 70. Full preterists agree with partial preterists here, but add that the coming, gathering and judgment that follow it in the same passages happened at that time too. No future tribulation remains.

Using the day-year principle, historicists read the 1,260 days or 42 months as 1,260 years of the church's suffering under apostate power. A common reckoning for the papacy is AD 538 to 1798. The great tribulation is thus spread through church history, especially the persecution of faithful witnesses by Rome.
Historicists vary widely on start and end dates for the 1,260 years.

Revelation 6-19 describes a future period of judgment just before Christ returns, usually identified with Daniel's seventieth week. The numbers in Revelation 11-13 (1,260 days, 42 months) mark its halves. Most futurists see an end-time crisis of unprecedented intensity.
Non-dispensational futurists (Ladd) expect a future tribulation of undetermined length (future-final).

Tribulation is the normal experience of the church in every age, as John shared it with his readers. The 'great tribulation' of Revelation 7:14 is the whole span of suffering out of which the redeemed come. Idealists allow that this conflict may reach a final climax before the end.

Beale reads tribulation as beginning with Christ's sufferings and continuing through the whole age, in which believers already share. It also points to an intensified final period just before the end. The first-century persecution John's readers faced is a real instance of it.

Many contemporary postmillennialists identify the beast of Revelation 13 as Nero, whose name in Hebrew letters gives 666. They link the man of lawlessness to the first-century apostasy and judgment, not to a future world ruler. John's 'many antichrists' were first-century heretics.
Older (historicist) postmillennialists, including the Westminster divines, identified the pope as Antichrist (papacy); modern postmillennialists vary.

The spirit of antichrist has been active since the apostles' day and appears in persecuting states and false teachers in every age. Many amillennialists expect it to culminate in a final personal Antichrist, the man of lawlessness, whom Christ destroys at his coming. Others place more weight on the recurring pattern than on a single individual.
Reformation-era amillennialists commonly identified the papacy as Antichrist (papacy).

A personal Antichrist will arise at the end of the age, persecute the church and be destroyed by Christ at his return. Historic premillennialists see this already in the early church, as with Irenaeus. The beast of Revelation 13 may draw on first-century Rome, but it finds its ultimate fulfilment in this final figure.

The Antichrist is a future individual, the 'prince who is to come' of Daniel 9:26-27. He will rise from a revived Roman empire, make and break a seven-year covenant with Israel, and demand worship in a rebuilt temple. He rules the world during the tribulation until Christ destroys him.

Revelation was written for first-century readers about things that would shortly take place. Partial preterists therefore identify the beast as Nero Caesar, whose name transliterated into Hebrew gives 666 and whose persecution lasted about 42 months, and the beast's seven heads with Rome's seven hills and emperors. The man of lawlessness is a first-century figure tied to the temple's destruction.

Disputed in its details: preterists identify the man of lawlessness variously with Nero, Titus, or the Jewish rebel leaders. The early date of Revelation (before AD 70) on which this reading relies is disputed; most scholars favour c. AD 95.

Full preterists identify the beast with Nero or the Roman power of the 60s. They see John's 'many antichrists' as first-century deniers of Christ and the man of lawlessness as a figure of the apostasy that ended in AD 70. No future Antichrist remains to be revealed.

From the Reformation onward, historicists identified the man of lawlessness and the beast with the papacy. They saw an apostate power seated in the church's temple, ruling for 1,260 prophetic years and claiming divine prerogatives. Many also read Islam in the locusts and horsemen of the fifth and sixth trumpets.
Luther, Calvin, and the original Westminster Confession (25.6) identified the pope as Antichrist; later Westminster-derived confessions removed that clause.

The beast of Revelation 13 is a future world ruler who will head a final empire, make war on the saints, and be destroyed at Christ's return. His career fills the end-time period of Revelation 6-19. Futurists usually identify him with Daniel's little horn and Paul's man of lawlessness.

The sea beast stands for anti-Christian political power and persecuting government in every age. The land beast, or false prophet, stands for false religion and ideology that serve such power. Rome was the first-century embodiment, but the beast reappears whenever the state claims divine honour.
Many idealists (e.g. Hendriksen) also allow for a final personal Antichrist (principle-with-final-person).

Beale reads the beast as Rome in John's day and as the recurring state power that opposes Christ throughout the age. He also expects it to reach a final, intensified form at the end. Eclectic interpreters hold the first-century, transhistorical and future dimensions together.

Elsewhere in Matthew, 'this generation' always means Jesus' contemporaries (for example Matthew 23:36). Many postmillennialists therefore hold that the signs and the judgment-coming of Matthew 24:4-34 were fulfilled by AD 70. Many see verse 36 as the turn to the unknown day of the final return.
Postmillennialists differ on where the transition falls (24:36, 25:31, or nowhere in the discourse). Older postmillennialists did not always take the preterist reading.

Most amillennialists take 'this generation' to mean Jesus' contemporaries, who saw the temple destroyed. They also see the discourse as blending, in prophetic perspective, the judgment of AD 70 with the end of the age. The fall of Jerusalem is the first fulfilment and a type of the final coming.
Hoekema leaned toward reading genea as the rebellious Jewish people (race-or-kind); some amillennialists are fully preterist on Matthew 24:4-34.

'This generation' most naturally means Jesus' hearers. Historic premillennialists such as Ladd and Blomberg relate it to the events leading up to AD 70, while holding that the discourse also looks past them to the coming of the Son of Man. Ladd described the blend as prophetic 'telescoping'.

Dispensationalists such as Walvoord and Ice read 'this generation' as the generation alive when the signs of the end-time tribulation begin. That generation will see everything through to Christ's return. The discourse answers Jewish disciples' questions about Israel's future in Daniel's seventieth week.
C. I. Scofield took genea as 'race', meaning the Jewish nation would be preserved until the end (race-or-kind).

Jesus said his own generation would see 'all these things'. So the abomination, the tribulation, the darkened sun (covenantal judgment language) and the coming on the clouds were fulfilled in the judgment of AD 70, vindicating the Son of Man. Most partial preterists see a shift to the final, unknown day at Matthew 24:36 or 25:31.
N. T. Wright reads all of Mark 13 as about AD 70 while holding a future return on other grounds.

'This generation' means Jesus' contemporaries, and 'all these things' includes the coming of the Son of Man, the gathering of the elect and the end of the age. Full preterists argue there is no textual break, so the entire discourse was fulfilled by AD 70. They hold that the end of the age was the end of the old covenant age.

Historicist commentators such as Albert Barnes held that 'this generation' refers to people then living, who saw Jerusalem destroyed in AD 70. They read the parts of the discourse about the final coming as reaching beyond that into the church's history. The first fulfilment was a pledge of the rest.

Futurists generally read 'this generation' as the generation that witnesses the signs of the end, because the coming of the Son of Man in Matthew 24:30 did not visibly happen in AD 70. They agree that the discourse may also address Jerusalem's fall. They argue that its climax is still future.
Non-dispensational futurists such as Ladd prefer the contemporaries-dual reading.

Idealism is an approach to Revelation and does not, by itself, settle how to read the Olivet Discourse. Idealist commentators usually take 'this generation' as Jesus' contemporaries for the fall of Jerusalem. They treat that judgment as a pattern for judgments repeated through the age and for the final coming.
The stance given is the one typical of idealist (mostly amillennial) commentators.

Eclectic interpreters usually see Jesus' generation fulfilling the core of the discourse in AD 70. They also see the final coming as both anticipated by that event and lying beyond it. This 'already and not yet' reading lets the first-century and future references stand together.

The seventy weeks run on without a break. The Messiah is 'cut off' within the seventieth week at the cross, and it is he who 'confirms a covenant with many' (the new covenant) and makes sacrifice cease by his once-for-all offering. The six goals of Daniel 9:24 (atonement, everlasting righteousness, anointing the most holy) are achieved in Christ's first coming. The desolation of Jerusalem in AD 70 is the announced consequence of rejecting him.
Postmillennialists differ on the start date (Cyrus, Artaxerxes) and on whether AD 70 falls inside or just after the seventieth week.

The numbers are symbolic: seventy sevens form a jubilee-shaped period of redemption centred on Christ. Christ is the anointed one who confirms the covenant. In the influential reading of Meredith Kline, the seventieth week begins with his ministry and its second half extends through the church age, matching Revelation's 'time, times and half a time'. There is no dispensational parenthesis. The church age is part of the prophecy, not an interruption of it.

Many amillennialists (E. J. Young and much older Reformed exegesis) hold the more chronological 'fulfilled in Christ' view shared with postmillennialists. Some older amillennial commentators (Keil, Leupold) placed a final Antichrist at the end of a symbolic scheme.

Many historic premillennialists see the prince who makes the covenant and sets up the abomination in Daniel 9:27 as an eschatological Antichrist, so at least part of the final week lies in the future. Jesus' use of Daniel in the Olivet Discourse and Paul's 'man of lawlessness' point to a final crisis before the return. They do not adopt the dispensational doctrine of a church-age parenthesis that separates Israel's programme from the church's.

Historic premillennialists vary widely. Posttribulationists such as Robert Gundry keep a future seventieth week, while others accept a messianic fulfilment of Daniel 9 and locate the future tribulation in other texts.

Sixty-nine weeks (483 years) ran exactly to Messiah the Prince, who was then 'cut off' after them. Daniel 9:26 places the destruction of the city before the seventieth week, which requires an interval. The 'he' of Daniel 9:27 is the coming prince, the Antichrist, who makes a seven-year covenant with Israel. Because the prophecy concerns Daniel's people and city, the seventieth week resumes after the church age as the future tribulation.

Dispensationalists differ in chronology. Sir Robert Anderson and Harold Hoehner counted 'prophetic years' of 360 days to reach Palm Sunday. Progressive dispensationalists keep the future seventieth week but soften the Israel/church parenthesis.

Daniel's prophecy is a unified, unbroken countdown, and inserting a two-thousand-year gap breaks its natural reading. The Messiah's death in the midst of the final week confirms the new covenant and ends the sacrificial system. The 'desolator' who comes on the wing of abominations is Rome in the Jewish War, and Jesus explicitly links this to his own generation.

Some partial preterists stretch the seventieth week to AD 70 itself, while Gentry treats AD 70 as the consequence of events within the week. Amillennial partial preterists may prefer a symbolic count.

The seventy weeks were determined to 'seal up vision and prophet', so all prophecy, including resurrection and judgment, had to be fulfilled when the seventy weeks ended. That end was the destruction of the city and sanctuary in AD 70, which Daniel 12:7 ties to the shattering of the holy people's power. To leave any part of the six goals of Daniel 9:24 unfulfilled is to break the prophecy's own time limit.

Full preterists vary in how they count the weeks. Critics from every other school reply that 'sealing up vision' refers to Christ fulfilling and authenticating prophecy at his first coming, not to the end of all prophetic fulfilment.

On the day-year principle, the seventy weeks are 490 literal years running from Artaxerxes' decree in 457 BC (Ezra 7). Week 69 ends with Christ's baptism (AD 27). He is cut off in the middle of the seventieth week (AD 31), and the week closes c. AD 34 when the gospel turns to the Gentiles. Historicists cite this precise fulfilment as the clearest confirmation of their method.
